title: False friends on the shooting ground
summary: Shooting words that look familiar but mean something else: smoke and dust, scoring words, “trap”, “stand” and “squad”, and pitfalls from French, Italian and Portuguese.

body.html: A false friend is a word that looks familiar but means something else on the shooting ground. Some of them change the score, so they are worth learning first.

The biggest pitfall is smoke. A coach’s “Smoked it!” (or “inked it”, “powdered it”) praises a perfect hit: the target vanished in a cloud. In the rules, a target that gives off only dust or smoke, with no visible piece, is a zero. A “chip”, a small visible piece, is a hit (one). “Dusted it” is risky: it can mean that only dust came off (a zero) or, for some coaches, a smashed target. So translate the coach’s “smoked it” as a full, clean hit and the referee’s “only dust” as a zero, and ask what “dusted it” means.

Scoring words are not literal. “Dead” and “kill” mean a hit, with nothing about death. “Lost” means a miss, not something lost. “Dropped two” means two targets missed. “Straight” in “25 straight” means a perfect run with no target missed.

Equipment and place words. A “trap” is the throwing machine, not a snare. A “stand” is a single shooting place, the shooting stand, not the whole ground; in Compak® Sporting the places are often called stations. A “peg” is the shooting position. The name comes from the numbered stake that marks each shooter’s place at a driven game shoot, so do not translate it as a stake. A “broken gun” is an open gun. “Pull!” is the call, “pull-away” is a lead method and “length of pull” is the length of the stock, from the trigger to the butt pad.

A “card” is a score card, or a yellow or red card. “On report” means at the sound of the shot, as in a double on report. A “squad” is the competition group of at most six shooters. ClayAway tours, which are coming soon, will also use the word for a sub-group of a tour.

Pairs have different names. A “true pair” (British and American) is a FITASC simultaneous double: both targets leave at the same time. A “report pair” is a double on report: the second target is launched by the sound of your first shot. A “following pair” is a FITASC rafale: two targets from the same trap, one right after the other. A “show pair” is the presentation of a pair before shooting. A “peg” is the shooting stand, “station” is the American word for a stand, and a “cage” is the frame around it.

Other languages have their own pitfalls. French “chandelle” is a target that springs almost straight up, which English calls a teal. It is not the English chandelle, a target that climbs steeply in a curve and then drops. French “en battue” and Italian “in battuta” mean driven game, not the battue target. In Portuguese, “batida” is the battue target, while “de batida” means driven. For a hit a French referee says “Bon” and an Italian “Buono”, and the trapper is often a “pulleur” or “puller”. Words for the squad also differ, so use the word of the event’s own rulebook.

key_points.html: Coach “smoked it” = perfect hit; rules “only dust or smoke” = zero
Dead / kill = hit; lost / dropped = miss; straight = perfect run
Trap = machine; stand = a single position; peg = the spot; broken gun = open gun
Pull, card, report and squad each have several meanings
French chandelle and “en battue” differ from the English words
True pair = simultaneous; report pair = on report; following pair = rafale

quiz.q: The coach shouts “Smoked it!” after a shot. What happened?

options.text: Only smoke came off: a zero
The target was destroyed: a perfect hit
The target was a flash target

quiz.explain: In coach slang “smoked it” is a perfect hit; in the rules “only dust or smoke” is a zero. The meanings are opposite.

quiz.q: The referee says “Lost.” What does it mean?

options.text: The target flew out of sight
The shooter ran out of time
The target left its usual line
A miss: the target is a zero

quiz.explain: “Lost” is the scoring word for a miss (zero), not something lost.

quiz.q: A French guest says he loves shooting “en battue”. What does he mean?

options.text: Driven game (birds driven over the guns)
The thin battue target that turns
A target thrown as part of a pair
A target that breaks into dust

quiz.explain: French “en battue” (Italian “in battuta”) means driven game; the battue target is a separate thing.
